channel.name: 🐭-tinyqv
channel.topic:
**[TinyQV](https://thinyq.com)** by Mike Bell: a small RISC-V (RV32EC) SoC with peripherals from the Tiny Tapeout RISC-V competition, with chips on wafer.space runs.

**Run 1**
• [TQVA](https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVA.html) (0.5x0.5 slot)
• [TQVB](https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVB.html) (0.5x1 slot)
• [TQVC](https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVC.html) (1x0.5 slot)
**Run 2**
• [TQVA](https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVA.html) (0.5x0.5 slot)
• [TQVC](https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVC.html) (1x0.5 slot)
• [TQVD](https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVD.html) (HDMI output)
• [TQVE](https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVE.html) (experimental pad setup)
**Source**
• [tinyQV](https://github.com/MichaelBell/tinyQV)
• [ws01-tinyQV](https://github.com/MichaelBell/ws01-tinyQV) (Run 1)
• [ws02-tinyQV](https://github.com/MichaelBell/ws02-tinyQV) (Run 2)

messages.content:
To give some background:
TQVA/TQVB/TQVC were on run 1 and are identical designs, one in each of the quarter and half slot types. It’s a fairly minimal change over the Tiny Tapeout version, so the main IO is 8 inputs and 8 outputs (direction fixed), though UART and audio are broken out to separate pins.

I’ve proven TQVC works on a simpler host board which has the flash and RAM on a PMOD as in Tiny Tapeout. I designed a CoB for TQVA which matches the pinout of TQVC, and I believe I will very soon have 80 TQVA CoBs to test.

The design itself has peripherals for UART, SPI, PWM, SNES gamepads via the TinyTapeout PMOD, VGA out through the TinyTapeout PMOD, a couple of synths for audio, a couple of different programmable IO type blocks, and some other unusual peripherals from the Tiny Tapeout peripheral competition. It should make a decent platform for retro style games (but compiled with a modern toolchain).

On run 2 there were two new versions of TinyQV:
TQVD has an attempt at HDMI output, giving an 80x30 text mode with a scrollable full screen buffer (no need to race the beam!). The font has 32 programmable characters. The same display driver can also output VGA. IO is more flexible, GPIO can fully configure the 16 GPIO pins.

TQVE is an experiment with only 17 pads. That means it only has 6 GPIO, but it has a lot more on board scratch RAM. It also has a USB CDC peripheral, which will hopefully allow a serial console without needing an external UART adapter.

Both TQVD and TQVE use Tholin’s new cell library

I plan to order a simple host board for testing TQVD at the same time as the above board for TQVA/C.

@Andrew Wingate has kindly offered to create a CoB for TQVE which will be compatible with the TQVA/C pinout, so initial testing of that can be done with the existing host boards.
@RebelMike - There are some of your TinyQV boards with @algofoogle (Anton Maurovic) & @Greg here in Adelaide and with @Andrew Wingate in Chicago / Pumping Station 1

Awesome!  I can write up some bring-up instructions if that would be helpful to anyone.  I haven't tried bringing it up on a breadboard using the breadboard breakout but it should be possible.
Or the "v0" version of the host board is pretty cheap to get JLC to make (useful if you already have a Tiny Tapeout QSPI PMOD): https://codeberg.org/rebelmike/ws01-tinyQV-mobo-alpha/src/branch/v0
Or in a couple of weeks time I should have been able to verify the more fully featured one pictured above, which will obviously be a bit more expensive but should run standalone (though you'll still need a Pico or something to program it plus a UART adapter).

messages.content: Sure! My understanding is that Wafer Space will bond some TQVE to a CoB for me so I can check they work, but there will be plenty of bare dies so I'm very happy to send you (or for Tim to send you) some dies for experimentation!

Yeah there'll be the second batch afterwards anyways 😄
The flex PCB would be 2mil/2mil DRC from JLCPCB (2L 1/3oz special offer, except that the extended fine-structures below 3mil/3mil are ineligible for the 2$ offer and should cost about 17-ish $ instead).
I'll plan to rely on you for insight into the desired pinout/layout after/beyond what is inherently applicable to the ACF bonding aspects themselves?
Sure - at minimum it'll need clock and reset supplying, the QSPI pins connecting to a W25Q flash and a APS6404 PSRAM, and then GPIO 0 and 1 broken out for UART.

I haven't been following what the plan is for the flex PCB, is the idea to bond that to the chip and then to pads on a regular PCB?  So I could just design a variant of the regular host board with a suitable pad layout for it

Well, so, on the flex they come out from the die itself in the same order they are on the die, and IMO after they've left the die surface and a reasonable strain relief zone next to the right (SRAM) edge, then we can expand.
Also, the back/far layer has to be free of copper around the pads for visual alignment reasons; and IMO we might want to keep it pulled back on the entire die for starters (but not long-term).
you could put solder pads for your comfortable socket to a host board on it? Maybe pads to put decoupling capacitors close to the die?
Here's the first flex test for `FC01`; it's got a bit of coverlay-exclusion area to spare vs. the die outline; that's under 3mil/3mil DRCs. The flex in the image is 50x50mm.
(this has connections of traces to support 4-wire measurements of the bond resistance)
@RebelMike does it give you a decent scale/idea?

Yes I think so.  Just reading up on flex pcbs a bit - I've never looked at them before.  So given we just have 17 pads in a single row, we could just fan those out to a standard 2mm or 2.54mm pin socket to connect to a host PCB.  And as you say would make sense to put a decoupling cap on the flex pcb.

I'd probably think a cap to be good on it, yes.
The pin header on my upload there is 1.27mm pitch 2-row through-hole.
Or maybe a ZIF connector is the right solution
If you'd want. The flex is naturally too thin though; but due to the 2/2 bump adding a stiffener for ZIF wouldn't be much more on top IIRC
It looks like the pad pitch on TQVE is 102um so this would be super tight - you wouldn't be able to put a pad at all on the FPC, it would just be the 2mil trace.
yeah, that's normal for dense ACF usage, line pitch close to process minimums on one of the two sides (whichever has more trouble with fine pitch).

With this limitation and assuming to put power and gnd pads in the center instead, considering those don't really need the fancy stuff from the pad ring cells, a full slot should just about manage 148 IO's _I think._

Relies on CUP for the power and ground in the middle in practice though, IMO. Or "ab"-using the 4 corners to feed in through one large pad each that occupies almost all the area not in the way of the pad fanout traces and between sealring and power-ring-corner-cell.
Opps, seems @Andrew Wingate already forwarded this...
I've put a super basic webpage up for TinyQV at https://tinyqv.com, mostly just a collection of links for now.

# Welcome to #🐭-tinyqv
This channel is for **TinyQV**, @RebelMike's (Mike Bell) small RISC-V SoC, first built for Tiny Tapeout, and the chips made on wafer.space runs. @RebelMike looks after this channel.

**Chips**
- Run 1: [TQVA](<https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVA.html>), [TQVB](<https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVB.html>) and [TQVC](<https://wafer.space/ws-run1/projects/TQVC.html>)
- Run 2: [TQVA](<https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVA.html>), [TQVC](<https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVC.html>), [TQVD](<https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVD.html>) (HDMI output) and [TQVE](<https://wafer.space/ws-run2/projects/TQVE.html>) (experimental pad setup)

**Source**
- [tinyQV](<https://github.com/MichaelBell/tinyQV>): the core, for Tiny Tapeout
- [ws01-tinyQV](<https://github.com/MichaelBell/ws01-tinyQV>): Run 1
- [ws02-tinyQV](<https://github.com/MichaelBell/ws02-tinyQV>): Run 2

If you have one of these chips, please post your bring-up results, boards, firmware and questions here.

I just received 50 of my TinyQV chip from Wafer Space!

The chips are tiny on the CoB!
